A significant portion of these are curated on the #IkoKaziKE hashtag, which has since spread to other social media sites.</p><p><strong>Rose Munuhe, a marketer in Nairobi who started the hashtag in December 2016, told The Africa Report</strong> she never thought it would become what it is now. “I had just resigned from my job and reality was dawning, it is pretty hard to find a job,” she explained, “It solved a problem most job sites seem to have not figured out which is: Feedback gives job seekers hope.”</p><ul><li>Munuhe has a similarly named career blog “…that features many youths and their success stories giving hope to the rest and sharing their career experiences for all those looking to know more.”</li></ul><p></p><div class="twitter-tweet twitter-tweet-rendered" style="display: flex; max-width: 500px; width: 100%; margin-top: 10px; margin-bottom: 10px;"><iframe id="twitter-widget-2" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" allowtransparency="true" allowfullscreen="true" class="" title="X Post" src="https://platform.twitter.com/embed/Tweet.html?creatorScreenName=theafricareport&dnt=true&embedId=twitter-widget-2&%3D%3D&frame=false&hideCard=false&hideThread=false&id=1135826909831606272&lang=en&origin=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.theafricareport.com%2F13844%2Fkenya-can-a-hashtag-save-the-job-market%2F&sessionId=bcb390e7d2899002128de172c8ab76f9ba9f570b&siteScreenName=theafricareport&theme=light&widgetsVersion=6a3ad42b224df%3A1778106238597&width=500px" style="position: absolute; visibility: hidden; width: 0px; height: 0px; display: block; flex-grow: 1;" data-tweet-id="1135826909831606272"></iframe></div><blockquote class="twitter-tweet" data-width="500" data-dnt="true" data-twitter-extracted-i1792092782625557787="true"><p lang="en" dir="ltr"><a href="https://twitter.com/hashtag/IkoKaziKE?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#IkoKaziKE</a> UBA Kenya is looking for a Credit Analyst. A virtual referral system that says that your digital presence/platform may be where I gain my next customer and all you have to donate, even to a stranger, is an implicit endorsement, the retweet,” says Kaigwa.</li></ul><p><strong>Outside the hashtag, young Kenyans are also engaging in well-calculated stunts</strong> both online and offline to get noticed.</p><ul><li>In 2017, a man made news after walking around Nairobi with a placard bearing his image, credentials, and phone number. He got a job, before<a href="https://www.tuko.co.ke/269559-nairobi-man-placard-a-job-quits-employment-20k-salary.html#269559" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> quitting a year later over low pay</a>.</li><li>At this year’s Labor Day celebrations, another man spent his time <a href="https://www.capitalfm.co.ke/news/2019/05/jobless-graduates-desperate-attempt-to-seek-a-job-at-labour-day-fete/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">holding a similar placard</a>. He later told reporters that he had decided “to put this banner on their faces so that someone can at least spot me.”</li><li>After 27-year-old Ruth Jemutai’s unsuccessful job hunt was highlighted by a media house, she got multiple job offers, eventually accepting a government job with the energy regulator.</li><li>A senior government official, Interior Permanent Secretary Karanja Kabicho, was<a href="https://nairobinews.nation.co.ke/news/uhuru-settles-small-debt-he-owed-chewing-gum-hawker" target="_blank" rel="noopener"> ‘forced’ to settle a Shs. 40 debt</a> that President Kenyatta owed to a hawker who sold him chewing gum in September 2017.</li></ul><p>For Rose Munuhe, the hashtag expands information on the few opportunities available, and helps young Kenyans share stories of the job market. “Since #IkoKaziKE started Kenyans on Twitter help one another tag jobs, they use the hash tag to recruit, share testimonials and work related advice,” she says.</p><p><strong>But, but, but:</strong> Kenya’s unemployment crisis requires structural solutions, she says. “A hashtag can’t save this.”</p>
